title: Atrial myxoma removal: operative lecture (Prof. Dr. Tolga Demir)

overlays.text: Myxoma: commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults
Commonest malignant: angiosarcoma, usually right atrium
75% left atrium, fossa ovalis border; women, age 40 to 60
Villous type embolises; smooth type obstructs
Triad 2 - Embolism in 30-40%: brain, retina, limbs
Triad 3 - Fever, weight loss, anaemia, high ESR (IL-6)
Heparin 300-400 U/kg; ACT > 400-480 s for bypass
Over-retraction: rib fracture, brachial plexus injury
TTE finds most myxomas; TEE best for the attachment
RULE: minimal handling before the cross-clamp
Differential: LA thrombus (appendage, AF, mitral stenosis)
Over 40 or risk factors: coronary angiography (tumour blush)
Right atrial myxoma: tricuspid obstruction, pulmonary emboli
Cannulation risks: bleeding, air, atheroma, dissection
Circuit: reservoir, pump, oxygenator, filter, cannulas
Bicaval cannulation isolates the right atrium
Haematocrit on bypass: keep above about 20-24%
No left heart vent: it could break up the tumour
Caution: right pulmonary artery behind the SVC
Before the clamp, fragments embolise systemically
Triangle of Koch = AV node: avoid (heart block)
Myxoma is friable: stay away from it
Histology: stellate cells, myxoid stroma; calretinin +
Very thin septum: closed with a pledget
Large defect: pericardial or synthetic patch
CO2 field flooding; TEE to detect air
Cerebral air: stroke, confusion; hyperbaric O2 if severe
Coronary air: right coronary artery (ST elevation)
AF prophylaxis: beta-blockers, K and Mg, amiodarone
Carotids pressed to protect the brain from air
Protamine 1 mg per 100 U heparin, given slowly
Re-exploration for bleeding: a few percent
Stroke risk: tumour fragments and air
Follow-up echo: before discharge, then yearly; familial lifelong
Exam: commonest adult tumour, LA septum, triad, echo, excise base
Keys: minimal handling, no LA vent, discard suction, excise base, de-air

questions.question: What did the echocardiogram before surgery show?
options: A giant tumour attached to the atrial septum, moving in and out of the mitral valve
A vegetation on the aortic valve
A thrombus in the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation: The echo caption says a giant cardiac tumour (myxoma) attached to the atrial septum was moving in and out of the mitral valve in a 60-year-old woman.

questions.question: Which is the commonest cardiac tumour in children?
questions.explanation: Rhabdomyoma is the commonest cardiac tumour in children and is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis. Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults.

questions.question: Which type of myxoma is most prone to embolism?
questions.explanation: Villous, papillary myxomas are friable and embolise more often; smooth, solid tumours tend to obstruct.

questions.question: How can a left atrial myxoma mimic mitral stenosis?
options: By obstructing mitral inflow in diastole
questions.explanation: A prolapsing tumour obstructs flow through the mitral orifice, causing breathlessness, orthopnoea and pulmonary oedema that may vary with posture.

questions.question: Roughly how often do left-sided myxomas cause systemic embolism?
questions.explanation: Embolism occurs in roughly 30 to 40 percent, most often to the brain, but also to the retina, coronary arteries, kidneys and limbs.

questions.question: How does heparin prevent clotting in the bypass circuit?
options: It potentiates antithrombin, inactivating thrombin and factor Xa
questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin and greatly speeds its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa. Typical dose for bypass: 300 to 400 units per kilogram.

questions.question: What is a 'tumour plop'?
options: An early diastolic sound as the tumour strikes the ventricle
A systolic click from the mitral valve
A sound heard only on echo
questions.explanation: The mobile tumour moving into the ventricle in early diastole can produce this sound, with a diastolic murmur that varies with position.

questions.question: Which test best defines the attachment site of a myxoma?
questions.explanation: Transthoracic echo detects most myxomas; transoesophageal echo defines the attachment and finds small tumours even more accurately.

questions.question: Which principle governs this operation before the aorta is cross-clamped?
options: Minimal manipulation of the beating heart, to avoid dislodging tumour fragments
Early opening of the left atrium
Placing a left ventricular vent first
questions.explanation: Until the cross-clamp is on, any fragment would embolise straight into the systemic arteries, so the heart is handled as little as possible.

questions.question: Where does left atrial thrombus usually lie, unlike a myxoma?
options: In the left atrial appendage, typically with AF or mitral stenosis
On the interatrial septum by a stalk
questions.explanation: Thrombus favours the appendage in patients with atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis; a myxoma is typically mobile and attached to the septum by a stalk.

questions.question: Before cannulating, the surgeon asks to be told when the ACT passes which value?
questions.explanation: Here cannulation starts after the ACT passes 300 seconds. Many teams require a longer ACT, often above 400 to 480 seconds, before full bypass.

questions.question: Where is the purse string labelled at 11:45 placed?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Vena kava superior kanul dikisi': the purse string for the superior caval cannula.

questions.question: Carney complex is most often caused by mutations in which gene?
questions.explanation: Carney complex is autosomal dominant and is usually caused by PRKAR1A mutations; it accounts for most familial myxomas.

questions.question: Which feature belongs to the Carney complex?
questions.explanation: Carney complex combines myxomas with spotty pigmentation, endocrine overactivity (such as Cushing syndrome from pigmented adrenal disease) and schwannomas.

questions.question: Which is a rare but serious complication of aortic cannulation?
questions.explanation: Dissection is suggested by a high arterial line pressure and a changing appearance of the aorta; other risks are bleeding, malposition and embolism of air or atheroma.

questions.question: Why are hypovolaemia and tachycardia avoided during anaesthesia in this patient?
options: They can worsen tumour obstruction of the mitral valve and cause collapse
questions.explanation: A tumour that obstructs mitral inflow can cause sudden hypotension on induction or with changes of position.

questions.question: Which vessel is cannulated in this minute?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Vena kava superior kanulasyonu'.

questions.question: How often is conventional blood cardioplegia usually repeated?
options: Only after the clamp is removed
questions.explanation: Conventional blood cardioplegia is re-dosed about every 15 to 20 minutes; single-dose solutions such as del Nido last much longer.

questions.question: How does bypass start in this case?
options: With both caval cannulas in place
With only the superior caval cannula draining, before the inferior caval cannula is placed
After the right atrium is opened
questions.explanation: 'Start. One cannula for now.' The inferior caval cannula is added next.

questions.question: What is the purse string placed low on the right atrium for?
questions.explanation: 'The stitch for the inferior cava': it will hold the inferior caval cannula.

questions.question: What is a typical full-bypass pump flow?
questions.explanation: Flows of about 2.2 to 2.5 litres per minute per square metre, with a mean arterial pressure of about 50 to 70 mmHg, are typical.

questions.question: Why is no left ventricular vent placed through the right superior pulmonary vein?
options: A vent passing through the left atrium could fragment the friable tumour and cause embolism
The pulmonary veins are too small
questions.explanation: 'We may not place a vent here, because I don't want to break up the mass.' The heart is decompressed through the aortic root instead.

questions.question: Which structure can be injured when a tape is passed around the superior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The right pulmonary artery lies behind the superior vena cava; injury to it or to the cavae is a recognised cause of bleeding.

questions.question: During this minute the heart is still beating. What will stop it?
questions.explanation: The cross-clamp isolates the coronary circulation and cardioplegia arrests the heart.

questions.question: How does high-potassium cardioplegia arrest the heart?
options: It depolarises the myocardial cell membrane, causing diastolic arrest and lowering oxygen demand
It hyperpolarises the membrane and causes systolic arrest
It cools the heart to 4 degrees by itself
questions.explanation: Raised extracellular potassium depolarises the membrane and inactivates sodium channels, so the heart stops in diastole. Topical cold saline adds protection while the patient stays normothermic.

questions.question: What happens when the caval snares are tightened at 25:35?
questions.explanation: All venous blood now goes to the machine: 'now we're on full bypass'.

questions.question: Through which chamber does the surgeon first enter the heart?
options: The left atrium through Sondergaard's groove
questions.explanation: A right atriotomy (label 'Atriyotomi') gives access to the interatrial septum.

questions.question: What does the triangle of Koch contain?
questions.explanation: Bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the septal tricuspid leaflet and the coronary sinus, it marks the AV node; excision near it risks heart block.

questions.question: Which landmark will the surgeon use to open the septum?
questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, is the thinnest part of the septum, and most left atrial myxomas arise near it.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon use the external (discard) suction near the tumour?
options: So tumour fragments go to waste and are not returned to the patient through the bypass circuit
questions.explanation: Blood from cardiotomy suction returns to the patient via the reservoir; discard suction keeps fragments out of the circuit.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon say 'Stay away from the mass'?
options: A myxoma is soft and friable, and touching it can break off fragments that embolise
The mass is calcified and blunts instruments
It is not the real tumour
questions.explanation: Fragments of myxoma can embolise to the brain or other organs, so the tumour is handled as little as possible.

questions.question: Why is the tissue at the tumour's attachment removed too?
options: To leave no tumour behind and lower the risk of recurrence
questions.explanation: 'We'll take this part of the mass too.' Incomplete removal at the attachment is a cause of recurrence.

questions.question: Where was this myxoma attached?
questions.explanation: The echo report and the operation show attachment to the interatrial septum; its stalk is cut there (label 'Miksoma sapinin kesilmesi').

questions.question: Why is saline injected into the left ventricle after removal?
options: To test the mitral valve and make sure no tumour fragment remains
questions.explanation: 'Valve check. We make sure no piece is left inside' (label 'Mitral kapak kontrolu').

questions.question: Why is the septum closed with a pledget?
options: The septal tissue is very thin, and the pledget stops stitches cutting through and leaving a new ASD
To mark the site for echo
questions.explanation: 'Normally it can be closed without a pledget, but the tissue is very thin, so we don't want to create an ASD.'

questions.question: When would the septum need a patch instead of direct closure?
options: When a larger defect is created, for example by excising a full-thickness cuff of septum
Only when the tricuspid valve leaks
questions.explanation: Here only a limited septal incision was made, so it is closed directly (reinforced with a pledget). A full-thickness excision would leave a defect needing a pericardial or synthetic patch.

questions.question: Why do many surgeons flood the field with carbon dioxide?
options: CO2 is far more soluble in blood than air, so remaining bubbles dissolve quickly
questions.explanation: CO2 displaces air from the open heart; any residual bubbles dissolve much faster than air bubbles.

questions.question: What is the main danger of air left in the left heart when it restarts?
options: Air embolism to the brain or coronary arteries
questions.explanation: Air ejected from the left heart can block cerebral or coronary arteries, so careful de-airing is essential.

questions.question: Why are the lungs inflated by hand before the septum is fully closed?
options: To fill the left heart with blood and push out air
To give oxygen to the pump
questions.explanation: Manual ventilation pushes blood through the lungs into the left atrium, displacing air through the septal opening.

questions.question: Coronary air embolism most often affects which artery?
options: The right coronary artery, because it arises anteriorly
questions.explanation: Air rises to the anterior aortic root and enters the right coronary artery, causing transient right ventricular dysfunction and ST elevation.

questions.question: How often does a sporadic myxoma recur after complete excision?
options: Uncommonly, in the range of a few percent
Never, so no follow-up is needed
questions.explanation: Recurrence after complete excision of a sporadic myxoma is uncommon (a few percent); familial cases recur more often. Echocardiographic follow-up is recommended.

questions.question: How is the tricuspid valve tested?
options: Saline is injected into the right ventricle and the leaflets are watched as it fills
questions.explanation: 'Look, the heart is swelling. As it swells, the chordae pull' the leaflets together.

questions.question: How common is atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery?
options: Roughly a quarter to a third of patients, usually on day 2 to 3
questions.explanation: It is the commonest complication, treated with rate or rhythm control, and anticoagulation if it persists.

questions.question: How is complete heart block after surgery managed initially?
questions.explanation: Epicardial wires allow temporary pacing; persistent block may later need a permanent pacemaker.

questions.question: Why are the carotid arteries pressed when the cross-clamp comes off?
options: To reduce the chance of air reaching the brain
To stop bleeding from the neck
questions.explanation: Compressing the carotids briefly while the root is vented lowers the risk of cerebral air embolism.

questions.question: Which is a recognised adverse effect of protamine?
options: Hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions or pulmonary hypertension
questions.explanation: Protamine (about 1 mg per 100 units of heparin) is given slowly because of these reactions.

questions.question: How often does bleeding require re-exploration after cardiac surgery?
options: After a few percent of operations
questions.explanation: Re-exploration for bleeding or tamponade is needed after a few percent of cardiac operations.

questions.question: Which is a risk factor for deep sternal wound infection (mediastinitis)?
questions.explanation: Diabetes, obesity, chronic lung disease, smoking and prolonged ventilation raise the risk; incidence is roughly 1 to 2 percent.

questions.question: How is postpericardiotomy syndrome treated?
options: Anti-inflammatory drugs such as NSAIDs and colchicine
questions.explanation: It is an inflammatory reaction days to weeks after surgery, with fever, pleuritic pain and pericardial or pleural effusions.

questions.question: How are complete removal and the diagnosis confirmed after surgery?
questions.explanation: Postoperative echocardiography confirms complete removal and normal valve function; histopathology confirms myxoma (stellate cells in a myxoid stroma).

questions.question: When are screening for Carney complex and examination of relatives advised?
options: In familial or atypical cases, such as young patients, multiple or recurrent tumours, or unusual sites
Only if the tumour is in the right atrium
questions.explanation: Carney complex (often a PRKAR1A mutation) causes multiple, recurrent myxomas in younger patients; first-degree relatives should be examined.

questions.question: When do most myxoma recurrences appear?
options: Within the first few years, so echo is repeated yearly
questions.explanation: Echo before discharge and then yearly for several years; familial cases need lifelong surveillance.

questions.question: Which statement summarises this operation?
options: The myxoma was removed through the right atrium and septum on bypass, without a left heart vent, and both valves were checked
The tumour was removed through the aorta without bypass
The tumour was left in place and biopsied
questions.explanation: Bicaval cannulation, cardioplegic arrest, right atriotomy, transseptal excision with the stalk, fragment and valve checks, careful de-airing.

narration.text: Welcome to this operative lecture on the excision of a left atrial myxoma, filmed from the surgeon's point of view, with Professor Tolga Demir operating.
We will follow every step, and use the quieter moments to review pathology, diagnosis, surgical principles, and complications.
The preoperative echocardiogram, in a sixty year old woman, shows a large mass attached to the interatrial septum that prolapses through the mitral orifice in diastole.

Primary cardiac tumours are rare, found in well under one in a thousand autopsies, and metastases to the heart are far more common. Most primary tumours are benign, and in adults myxoma accounts for about half of them.

Other benign tumours include papillary fibroelastoma, the commonest tumour of the heart valves, lipoma, fibroma, and rhabdomyoma, the commonest cardiac tumour in children, which is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis. The commonest primary malignant tumour in adults is angiosarcoma, which typically arises in the right atrium.

Myxomas occur more often in women, usually between the fourth and sixth decades. About three quarters arise in the left atrium, and most of the rest in the right atrium. The typical site is the interatrial septum at the border of the fossa ovalis, exactly as in this patient.

A myxoma is thought to arise from multipotent mesenchymal cells beneath the endocardium. It is usually pedunculated and gelatinous. Smooth, solid tumours tend to obstruct, while villous, papillary tumours are friable and embolise more often.
An iodine impregnated incise drape covers the operative field.
Skin incision. A median sternotomy gives full access to the heart, the great vessels and both venae cavae.

Clinically, myxomas present with a classic triad. First, obstruction. A left atrial tumour can obstruct mitral inflow and mimic mitral stenosis, with breathlessness, orthopnoea and pulmonary oedema. Symptoms may change with posture, and syncope or sudden death can occur when the tumour wedges in the valve.

Second, embolism, which occurs in roughly thirty to forty percent of patients with left sided tumours, most often to the brain, but also to the retina, the coronary arteries, the kidneys and the limbs. Third, constitutional features: fever, weight loss, fatigue, joint pain, anaemia and a raised sedimentation rate, driven largely by interleukin six released by the tumour.

On investigation, the electrocardiogram and chest X ray are often non specific, but may show left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion. Blood tests may show anaemia, a raised C reactive protein and sedimentation rate, and raised immunoglobulins.
Ventilation is suspended during the sternotomy, so the lungs fall away from the saw and the pleura is spared.
Ventilation resumes. The bone looks thin, so the sternal edges are handled gently to avoid a fracture.

Systemic heparin is given, typically three hundred to four hundred units per kilogram. Heparin potentiates antithrombin, which inactivates thrombin and factor ten a, and so prevents clotting in the extracorporeal circuit.

Bone wax provides mechanical haemostasis at the cut marrow. A rare but important complication of heparin is heparin induced thrombocytopenia, which requires an alternative anticoagulant such as bivalirudin.
The activated clotting time, the A C T, will be measured about three minutes after the heparin.

On examination, a myxoma may produce a tumour plop, an early diastolic sound as the mass strikes the ventricle, with a diastolic murmur that varies with position. The sternal retractor is opened gradually, because excessive spreading can fracture ribs and stretch the brachial plexus.
Without treatment, a myxoma can cause sudden death from valvular obstruction or a major embolus, which is why surgery should not be delayed once the diagnosis is made.
Pericardiotomy. The pericardium is opened in the midline.

As the surgeon anticipated, there is a considerable pericardial effusion, which is aspirated. Transthoracic echocardiography detects most myxomas, and transoesophageal echocardiography defines the attachment site and detects small tumours even more accurately.
On echocardiography, a myxoma is usually a mobile, heterogeneous mass with a narrow stalk, sometimes with small cystic or calcified areas, prolapsing through the mitral valve in diastole.

Pericardial stay sutures suspend the pericardium and elevate the heart. Cardiac magnetic resonance and computed tomography help to characterise the mass and to distinguish it from thrombus or a malignant tumour.

Note the principle that governs this whole operation: minimal manipulation of the heart before the aorta is clamped, because handling the beating heart could dislodge fragments of this friable tumour. The main differential diagnosis is left atrial thrombus, which usually lies in the appendage in patients with atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis, whereas a myxoma is typically mobile and attached to the septum by a stalk. In patients over about forty, or with risk factors, coronary angiography is done before surgery, and it may show a vascular blush within the tumour.

Other differential diagnoses include papillary fibroelastoma, a small frond like tumour on the valves that can also cause stroke, the vegetations of infective endocarditis, and malignant tumours, which tend to have a broad base, invade surrounding structures and cause bloody pericardial effusions.
Purse string sutures are now placed for cannulation. They secure each cannula, and close the opening when it is removed.
The first goes on the distal ascending aorta. In an atherosclerotic aorta, epiaortic ultrasound helps to choose a safe site, because cannulating or clamping through plaque can cause a stroke.
The surgeon asks to be told when the A C T exceeds three hundred seconds. Before full bypass, most teams require values above four hundred to four hundred and eighty seconds.
The A C T is a whole blood test of the intrinsic and common pathways. Heparin resistance, often due to low antithrombin, may need more heparin or antithrombin concentrate.
A second purse string goes on the superior vena cava. Direct caval cannulation, rather than a single atrial cannula, keeps the right atrium free to be opened.
Right atrial myxomas behave differently. They can obstruct the tricuspid valve, cause right heart failure, and embolise to the lungs rather than to the systemic circulation.

Snares are threaded over the purse strings. Familial myxoma, about five to ten percent of cases, is part of the Carney complex, an autosomal dominant syndrome usually caused by mutations in the P R K A R one A gene.
Ventricular myxomas are rare, and are more common in familial cases, where tumours may also be found in more than one chamber.

The clotting time has passed three hundred. Carney complex combines cardiac myxomas with spotty skin pigmentation, endocrine overactivity such as Cushing syndrome from pigmented adrenal disease, and schwannomas. Its myxomas are often multiple, appear in younger patients and in unusual sites, and recur more often.
The inferior caval cannula is prepared, and then the aortic cannula.
The systolic pressure is checked. Cannulating at a lower pressure reduces the risk of aortic dissection.
The aortic cannula is inserted, snared and tied.

Complications of aortic cannulation include bleeding, malposition, embolism of atheroma or air, and rarely iatrogenic aortic dissection, suggested by a high line pressure and a changing appearance of the aorta.

The arterial line is connected without air, because even small volumes of air in the arterial circuit can cause cerebral air embolism. Remember the anaesthetic concerns as well: a tumour that obstructs the mitral valve can cause sudden hypotension on induction or with changes of position, so hypovolaemia and tachycardia are avoided.

The bypass circuit consists of the venous cannulas and tubing, a reservoir, a pump, an oxygenator with a heat exchanger, an arterial filter and the arterial cannula. Cardiotomy suckers return shed blood to the reservoir, while a discard sucker sends it to waste.
The superior vena cava is cannulated, and the cannula is snared and secured.
Venous cannulas are sized to the patient, so that drainage is unobstructed at full flow.

Consider why bicaval cannulation matters here. With a single atrial cannula, opening the right atrium would let air into the venous line and flood the field. Two snared caval cannulas isolate the right atrium completely. Venous blood drains to the machine by gravity, often assisted by gentle vacuum, while the arterial pump returns oxygenated blood to the aorta.

Haemodilution from the circuit prime lowers the haematocrit, and many teams aim to keep it above about twenty to twenty four percent during bypass. Temperature, urine output, blood gases and venous oxygen saturation are monitored continuously by the perfusionist and the anaesthetist.

A cardioplegia cannula is placed in the ascending aorta, proximal to the future cross clamp. Cardioplegia can be crystalloid or blood based. Conventional blood cardioplegia is repeated about every fifteen to twenty minutes, while single dose solutions such as del Nido last much longer.
The adequacy of myocardial protection is judged later by how quickly the heart recovers, by the need for inotropes, and by any new wall motion abnormality or rhythm disturbance.
Cardiopulmonary bypass begins with superior caval drainage alone.
Meanwhile, a purse string is placed low on the right atrium for the inferior caval cannula.
Partial bypass at this stage unloads the heart while it continues to beat and eject.
During partial bypass the heart still ejects, so gentle ventilation continues until full flow is reached.

With the inferior caval cannula in place, bicaval drainage is established. On full bypass, flows of about two point two to two point five litres per minute per square metre are typical, with a mean arterial pressure of about fifty to seventy millimetres of mercury.
Venous drainage can fail if a cannula is kinked, malpositioned or contains an air lock, and the perfusionist reports a falling reservoir level at once.
Venous return is checked and full flow is reached, so ventilation stops. Bypass itself triggers a systemic inflammatory response, and it dilutes the blood and the clotting factors.
These effects can contribute to bleeding, fluid retention, and lung and kidney dysfunction after surgery.

A key decision: no left ventricular vent through the right superior pulmonary vein. A vent passed through the left atrium could fragment the tumour and cause embolism, so the heart will be decompressed through the aortic root instead.
In most other operations, a left ventricular vent through the right superior pulmonary vein is routine, so this change is deliberate and specific to myxoma.

Tapes are passed around both venae cavae. Tightening them will divert all venous return into the cannulas. Injury to the cavae, or to the right pulmonary artery behind the superior vena cava, is a recognised cause of bleeding during this step.
Some surgeons approach large myxomas through both atria, which allows the tumour to be removed with minimal traction and the whole septum to be inspected.
The inferior vena cava is dissected carefully.
Until the aorta is clamped, any fragment that breaks off would travel straight into the systemic arteries. That is why the heart is handled so little up to this point.
If the tumour obstructs the mitral valve severely, the circulation can deteriorate abruptly before bypass, so the team is always ready to go on bypass quickly.
The aortic cross clamp is applied between the aortic cannula and the cardioplegia site.
Pump flow is reduced briefly while the clamp is applied, to protect the aortic wall. Cardioplegia is then infused into the aortic root.

Diastolic arrest follows. High potassium cardioplegia depolarises the myocardial cell membrane and stops electromechanical activity, lowering oxygen demand. Topical cold saline adds protection, while the patient is kept normothermic.

Myocardial protection reduces oxygen demand through arrest and cooling, and supplies substrate with each dose of cardioplegia. Inadequate protection shows as low cardiac output after the cross clamp is removed.
The caval snares are tightened. This is total cardiopulmonary bypass. From now on the heart depends on myocardial protection, so the team keeps track of the ischaemic time.
With total bypass, the right atrium can be opened without air entering the venous lines.
Right atriotomy. The right atrium is opened.
Right atriotomies are generally placed away from the sinus node at the junction with the superior vena cava, to reduce the risk of sinus node dysfunction.
If more exposure were needed, the incision could be extended toward the aorta.

Stay sutures retract the atrial wall. Inside the right atrium, the triangle of Koch, bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the coronary sinus, marks the atrioventricular node.
The aortic root vent decompresses the heart, and the cardioplegia line is clamped. Excision close to the triangle of Koch risks heart block, one of the rare complications of septal tumour resection.
Sinus node dysfunction and junctional rhythms after atrial surgery are usually temporary, and are supported with atrial pacing.
The septal landmarks are identified. The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, and the thinnest part of the septum.
The septum primum forms the floor of the fossa, and the limbus, its muscular rim, surrounds it.

Alternative approaches include a left atriotomy through Sondergaard's groove, a biatrial approach, and minimally invasive right mini thoracotomy with femoral cannulation and video or robotic assistance.
The choice depends on the size and site of attachment, and on the surgeon's experience.
Here is the fossa ovalis, with the tumour visible behind it in the left atrium. The surgeon asks for the external aspirator.

The septum is incised through the fossa ovalis. Notice that the surgeon repeatedly uses the external aspirator, a discard suction. Fluid aspirated near the tumour goes to waste instead of to the cardiotomy reservoir, so fragments cannot be returned to the patient through the bypass circuit.
Fragments left behind may implant on the endocardium, one proposed explanation for recurrence at a different site. Gentle technique and irrigation of the chambers reduce this risk.
Stay away from the mass. Myxomas are gelatinous and friable, and the villous, papillary type in particular tends to fragment and embolise.
The site of attachment is exposed with a small retractor.
The attachment is excised with the tumour. Complete removal of the base is the main safeguard against recurrence, and many surgeons excise a full thickness cuff of septum and repair it with a patch.
The depth of excision is balanced against creating a defect that must be patched, and against injury to the conduction tissue.
The stalk is divided at its septal attachment.
The tumour is delivered intact, without fragmentation.
The specimen: a lobulated, gelatinous mass with areas of haemorrhage. Histology typically shows stellate myxoma cells in a myxoid stroma rich in glycosaminoglycans.
The left ventricle is filled with saline to test mitral competence and to flush out any loose fragments.

No residual tumour is found. All four chambers should be inspected, because myxomas can be multiple, especially in familial cases. The specimen goes for histology, where immunostaining for calretinin supports the diagnosis.
Malignant cardiac tumours, unlike myxoma, are often not completely resectable and carry a much worse prognosis, which is why histological confirmation matters.
Because the septal tissue is thin, a felt pledget reinforces the suture line. It prevents the sutures from tearing through and creating an iatrogenic atrial septal defect.
The tricuspid valve will also be assessed before the right atrium is closed.
A pledget is a small piece of felt that spreads the tension of a stitch over a wider area of tissue.

Direct closure is possible because only a limited septal incision was made. A larger defect would need a pericardial or synthetic patch. A residual atrial septal defect is a recognised complication, detected by echocardiography after surgery.
Autologous pericardium is commonly used for septal patches. It handles well and is readily available.
The root vent is paused while the final septal sutures are placed.
While the left heart is open, the root vent and gentle suction keep the field dry without drawing tumour debris into the circuit.

Before the left heart is closed, it must be filled and de-aired, because air left behind is ejected when the heart starts to beat. Many surgeons also flood the field with carbon dioxide, which is far more soluble in blood than air, so remaining bubbles dissolve quickly. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows residual air in the left heart.

Air embolism to the brain can cause stroke, confusion or delayed waking. Prevention depends on complete filling of the heart before it ejects, venting of the aortic root, head down positioning, and careful removal of the cross clamp. Some centres use hyperbaric oxygen for severe cerebral air embolism.
Rewarming begins. Manual lung inflation drives blood from the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, displacing air through the septal opening before the last knot is tied.
Rewarming is gradual, avoiding a large gradient between the blood and the body, and avoiding overheating of the brain.
A slight head down position directs residual air away from the cerebral circulation.
Throughout this phase, the anaesthetist watches the transoesophageal echo for bubbles in the left atrium, the left ventricle and the aorta.

The knot is buried, so that no thrombogenic material remains exposed. Coronary air embolism typically affects the right coronary artery, which arises anteriorly, causing transient right ventricular dysfunction and S T elevation.
Right ventricular dysfunction from coronary air usually resolves with a higher perfusion pressure and a short period of support on bypass.
The septal closure is complete.
Recurrence after complete excision of a sporadic myxoma is uncommon, in the range of a few percent. Familial tumours recur much more often, up to about one in five, and need lifelong surveillance.
Multiple tumours at presentation and a young age are also associated with recurrence.
The tricuspid valve is tested by injecting saline into the right ventricle.
As the ventricle distends, the papillary muscles and chordae bring the leaflets into coaptation.
Only trace regurgitation is seen, so no repair is required. Moderate or severe regurgitation would usually be repaired with an annuloplasty ring.

The right atriotomy is closed. Now consider the complications after surgery. The commonest is atrial fibrillation, in roughly a quarter to a third of patients after cardiac surgery, typically on the second or third day. It is treated with rate or rhythm control, and with anticoagulation if it persists. Conduction disturbances, including complete heart block, are rare, and may need temporary pacing through epicardial wires.

Prophylaxis against atrial fibrillation includes continuing beta blockers, correcting potassium and magnesium, and amiodarone in selected patients. Atrial fibrillation persisting beyond about forty eight hours is considered for anticoagulation, because of the risk of stroke.
The heart is filled, and the inferior caval snare is released.
Before the clamp comes off, the heart is filled and the lungs are ventilated, so remaining air is pushed toward the root vent.
The cross clamp is removed with the aortic root vent on full suction, while the carotid arteries are briefly compressed to reduce the risk of cerebral air embolism.
Coronary reperfusion washes out the cardioplegia, and the heart resumes a spontaneous rhythm.
The patient is weaned from bypass, the cannulas are removed, and protamine reverses the heparin.
Protamine can cause hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions and, rarely, severe pulmonary hypertension, so it is given slowly.

Mediastinal drains are placed and haemostasis is confirmed. Bleeding that needs re-exploration occurs after a few percent of cardiac operations. The sternum is approximated with stainless steel wires.
Drain output is monitored closely in intensive care. Persistent high output, or signs of tamponade, lead to re-exploration.

Sternal stability is essential for healing. Deep sternal wound infection, or mediastinitis, occurs in roughly one to two percent of patients after sternotomy. Risk factors include diabetes, obesity, chronic lung disease, smoking and prolonged ventilation. It presents with fever, wound discharge and an unstable sternum, and needs debridement, antibiotics and often reconstruction.
Sternal precautions, avoiding heavy lifting and pushing for about six to eight weeks, allow the bone to heal.
Pericardial complications include early tamponade from bleeding, and late effusion a week or more after surgery, which can present with hypotension and low cardiac output, and needs drainage.
Classic signs of tamponade are hypotension, a raised venous pressure and falling urine output. After cardiac surgery the effusion may be localised, so echocardiography is essential.

The subcutaneous tissue is closed in layers, eliminating dead space. Postpericardiotomy syndrome, an inflammatory reaction days to weeks after surgery, causes fever, pleuritic chest pain and pericardial or pleural effusions, and responds to anti inflammatory drugs such as colchicine.
Most patients are extubated within hours of surgery and leave intensive care the next day.

After surgery, echocardiography confirms complete removal and normal valve function, and histopathology confirms the diagnosis. Stroke after cardiac surgery occurs in about one to two percent of patients, and here the added risks are tumour fragments and air.
Other complications include acute kidney injury, pneumonia and delirium, which are more common in older patients and after long bypass times.
The skin is closed with a continuous suture. Operative mortality for myxoma excision in modern series is low, and long term survival is excellent.
Long term, patients with a completely excised sporadic myxoma have a life expectancy close to that of the general population.

In familial or atypical cases, screening for the Carney complex and examination of first degree relatives are advised. Follow up includes echocardiography before discharge and then yearly for several years, because most recurrences appear within the first few years.

Remember the key exam points. Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults. Most arise from the left atrial septum. The triad is obstruction, embolism and constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis is by echocardiography. Treatment is prompt excision with the base. Recurrence is rare in sporadic cases, but common in the Carney complex.
The wound is dressed, with the drains exiting below the incision.
Most patients go home within about a week, with an echocardiogram before discharge.

To summarise: a left atrial myxoma was excised through a right atrial, transseptal approach, on bicaval cardiopulmonary bypass with cardioplegic arrest. The keys were minimal manipulation, no left heart vent, discard suction near the tumour, complete excision of the attachment, inspection for fragments, and meticulous de-airing.
Thank you for watching.
